question.text:
Which of the following congruences have precisely three solutions modulo $24?$

  1. $18x \equiv 12 \quad (\text{mod}\:24)$
  2. $9x \equiv 5 \quad (\text{mod}\:24)$
  3. $15x \equiv 18 \quad (\text{mod}\:24)$
question.explanation:
Recall the following facts regarding the congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n){:}$

  • The congruence has no solutions modulo $n$ if and only if \[ \text{gcd}(a,n) \!\not{|}\:b. \]

  • The congruence has $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)$ solutions modulo $n$ if and only if \[ \text{gcd}(a,n) \:{|}\:b. \]

With that in mind, let's examine our congruences.

  • Congruence I has six solutions modulo $24.$ We have $a=18$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(18,24)=6. \] Since $b=12$ is divisible by $6,$ this congruence has $6$ solutions.

  • Congruence II has no solutions. We have $a=9$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(9,24)=3. \] Since $b=5$ is not divisible by $3,$ this congruence has no solutions.

  • Congruence III has three solutions modulo $24.$ We have $a=15$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(15,24)=3. \] Since $b=18$ is divisible by $3,$ this congruence has $3$ solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Linear Congruences With Many Solutions

question.text:
Find the sum modulo $18$ of the solutions to the congruence $8x \equiv 14 \:(\text{mod}\:18).$

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=8$ and $n=18$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(8,18)=2. \] Since $b=14$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 8x &\equiv 14 && (\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 2\cdot4x &\equiv 2\cdot7 && (\text{mod}\:2\cdot9) \\[5pt] \cancel 2\cdot4x &\equiv \cancel 2\cdot7 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 2\cdot9) \\[5pt] 4x &\equiv 7 && (\text{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=4$ and $n_1=9$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(4,9)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $9.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $4\,(\textrm{mod}\:9).$ To find the inverse of $4\,(\textrm{mod}\:9),$ we compute the exponents of $4\,(\textrm{mod}\:9)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:9)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 4^2 &\equiv 16 \equiv 9+7\equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] 4^3 &\equiv 7 \cdot 4 \equiv 28\equiv 3\cdot 9 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \end{align*}

So, $4 \cdot 7 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:9),$ which means that $7$ is the multiplicative inverse of $4$ (modulo $9$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $7,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 4x &\equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] 7 \cdot 4x &\equiv 7 \cdot 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] (7 \cdot 4)x &\equiv 49 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 49 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 5\cdot 9 + 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 4 \: (\text{mod}\:9).$

But our original congruence was modulo $18$ (not modulo $9$). To find all the solutions modulo $18,$ we repeatedly add $9$ modulo $18$ until we reach the number $4$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] x_2&\equiv 4+9 \equiv 13 && (\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 13+9 \equiv {22} \equiv 1\cdot 18 + 4\equiv 4 \equiv x_1&& (\text{mod}\:18) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv 4, 13 \: (\text{mod}\:18).$

Finally,

\[4 + 13 \equiv 17 \quad (\text{mod}\:18). \]

question.text:
Find the solutions of $20x \equiv 8 \:(\text{mod}\:28).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $28,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=20$ and $n=28$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(20,28)=4. \] Since $b=8$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 20x &\equiv 8 && (\text{mod}\:28) \\[5pt] 4\cdot 5x &\equiv 4\cdot 2 && (\text{mod}\:4\cdot 7) \\[5pt] \cancel 4\cdot5x &\equiv \cancel 4\cdot2 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 4\cdot 7) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 2&& (\text{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in the new congruence, we have $a_1=5$ and $n_1=7$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(5,7)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $7.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:7).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:7),$ we compute the exponents of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:7)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:7)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 5^2 &\equiv 25 \equiv 3\cdot 7 + 4 \equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] 5^3 &\equiv 4 \cdot 5 \equiv 20 \equiv 2\cdot 7 + 6\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] 5^4 &\equiv 6 \cdot 5 \equiv 30 \equiv 4\cdot 7 +2 \equiv 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] 5^5 &\equiv 2 \cdot 5 \equiv 10 \equiv 1 \cdot 7 + 3 \equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] 5^6 &\equiv 3 \cdot 5 \equiv 15 \equiv 2\cdot 7 + 1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $3 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:7),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $7$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 5x &\equiv 3 \cdot 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] (3 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 6 \: (\text{mod}\:7).$

But our original congruence was modulo $28$ (not modulo $7$). To find all the solutions modulo $28,$ we repeatedly add $7$ modulo $28$ until we reach the number $6$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 6 && (\text{mod}\:28) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 6+7 \equiv 13 && (\text{mod}\:28) \\[5pt] x_3 & \equiv 13 + 7 \equiv 20 && (\text{mod}\:28) \\[5pt] x_4 & \equiv 20+ 7 \equiv 27 && (\text{mod}\:28) \\[5pt] x_5&\equiv 27+7 \equiv {34} \equiv 28 + 6 \equiv 6 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:28) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3,4}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{6}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{13}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{20} , \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{27}\: (\text{mod}\:28). \]

question.text:
Find the sum modulo $24$ of the solutions to the congruence $20x \equiv 12\:(\text{mod}\:24).$

question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=20$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(20,24)=4. \] Since $b=12$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 20x &\equiv 12 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[3pt] 4\cdot 5x &\equiv 4\cdot3 && (\text{mod}\:4\cdot6) \\[3pt] \cancel{4}\cdot 5x &\equiv \cancel{4}\cdot3 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel{4}\cdot6) \\[3pt] 5x &\equiv 3 && (\text{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in the new congruence, we have $a_1=5$ and $n_1=6$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(5,6)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $6.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:6).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:6),$ we compute the exponents of $6\,(\textrm{mod}\:10)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:6)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 5^2 \equiv 25 \equiv 4\cdot 6 + 1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

So, $5 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:6),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $6$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] 5 \cdot 5x &\equiv 5 \cdot 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] (5 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 15 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 15 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 2\cdot 6 + 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 3 \: (\text{mod}\:6). $

But our original congruence was modulo $24$ (not modulo $6$). To find all the solutions modulo $24,$ we repeatedly add $6$ modulo $24$ until we reach the number $3$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 3 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_2&\equiv 3+6 \equiv 9 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_3&\equiv 9+6 \equiv 15 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_4&\equiv 15+6 \equiv 21 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 21+6 \equiv {27} \equiv 24 + 3\equiv 3 \equiv x_1&& (\text{mod}\:24) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv 3, 9, 15,21 \: (\text{mod}\:24).$

Finally, \[ 3 + 9 + 15 + 21 \equiv 48 \equiv 2\cdot 24 \equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:24). \]

\begin{align*} 10x &\equiv 15 && (\text{mod}\:25) \\[3pt] 5\cdot2x &\equiv 5\cdot3 && (\text{mod}\:5\cdot5) \\[3pt] \cancel{5}\cdot2x &\equiv \cancel{5}\cdot3 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel{5}\cdot5) \\[3pt] 2x &\equiv 3 && (\text{mod}\:5) \end{align*}

Notice that in the new congruence, we have $a_1=2$ and $n_1=5$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(2,5)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $5.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:5).$ To find the inverse of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:5),$ we compute the exponents of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:5)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:5)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 2^2 &\equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] 2^3 &\equiv 4 \cdot 2 \equiv 8 \equiv 5+3 \equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] 2^4 &\equiv 3 \cdot 2 \equiv 6 \equiv 5+1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \end{align*}

So, $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:5),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $2$ (modulo $5$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 2x &\equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] 3 \cdot 2x &\equiv 3 \cdot 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] (3 \cdot 2)x &\equiv 9 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 9 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 5 + 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:5) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 4 \: (\text{mod}\:5).$

But our original congruence was modulo $25$ (not modulo $5$). To find all the solutions modulo $25,$ we repeatedly add $5$ modulo $25$ until we reach the number $4$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:25) \\[5pt] x_2&\equiv 4+5 \equiv 9&& (\text{mod}\:25) \\[5pt] x_3&\equiv 9+5 \equiv 14&& (\text{mod}\:25) \\[5pt] x_4&\equiv 14+5 \equiv 19&& (\text{mod}\:25) \\[5pt] x_5&\equiv 19+5 \equiv 24&& (\text{mod}\:25) \\[5pt] x_6 &\equiv 24+5 \equiv {29} \equiv 25 + 4\equiv 4 \equiv x_1&& (\text{mod}\:25) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 \: (\text{mod}\:25).$

Finally, \[ 4 + 9 + 14 + 19 + 24 \equiv 70 \equiv 2\cdot 25 + 20 \equiv 20 \quad (\text{mod}\:25). \]

example.title: Solving Linear Congruences With Many Solutions

question.text:
Find the solutions of $10x \equiv 35 \:(\text{mod}\:45).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $45,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=10$ and $n=45$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(10,45)=5. \] Since $b=35$ is divisible by $5,$ our congruence has $5$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 10x &\equiv 35 && (\text{mod}\:45) \\[5pt] 5\cdot2x &\equiv 5\cdot 7 && (\text{mod}\:5\cdot 9) \\[5pt] \cancel 5\cdot 2x &\equiv \cancel 5\cdot 7 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 5\cdot 9) \\[5pt] 2x &\equiv 7 && (\text{mod}\:9) \end{align*}

Notice that in the new congruence, we have $a_1=2$ and $n_1=9$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(2,9)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $9.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:9).$ To find the inverse of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:9),$ we compute the exponents of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:9)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:9)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 2^2 &\equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] 2^3 &\equiv 4 \cdot 2 \equiv 8 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] 2^4 &\equiv 8 \cdot 2 \equiv 16 \equiv 9+7 \equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9)\\[5pt] 2^5 &\equiv 7 \cdot 2 \equiv 14 \equiv 9+5 \equiv 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:9)\\[5pt] 2^6 &\equiv 5 \cdot 2 \equiv 10 \equiv 9+1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:9)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $5 \cdot 2 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:9),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $2$ (modulo $9$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 2x &\equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] 5 \cdot 2x &\equiv 5 \cdot 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] (5 \cdot 2)x &\equiv 35 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 35 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 3\cdot 9 + 8 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 8 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 8 \: (\text{mod}\:9).$

But our original congruence was modulo $45$ (not modulo $9$). To find all the solutions modulo $45,$ we repeatedly add $9$ modulo $45$ until we reach the number $8$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 8 && (\text{mod}\:45) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 8+9 \equiv 17 && (\text{mod}\:45) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 17+9 \equiv 26 && (\text{mod}\:45) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 26+9 \equiv 35 && (\text{mod}\:45) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 35+9 \equiv 44 && (\text{mod}\:45) \\[5pt] x_6&\equiv 44+9 \equiv {53} \equiv 45 + 8 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:45) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3,4,5}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{8}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{17},\: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{26},\: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{35},\: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{44} \: (\text{mod}\:45). \]

question.text:
Find the solutions of $185 x \equiv 35 \:(\text{mod}\:575).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $575,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(185,575) =5.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=185$ and $n=575$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(185,575)=5. \] Since $b=35$ is divisible by $5,$ our congruence has $5$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 185x &\equiv 35 && (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] 5\cdot 37x &\equiv 5\cdot 7 && (\text{mod}\:5\cdot 115) \\[5pt] \cancel 5\cdot 37x &\equiv \cancel 5\cdot 7 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 5\cdot 115) \\[5pt] 37x &\equiv 7 && (\text{mod}\:115) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=37$ and $n_1=115$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(37,115)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $115.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $37\,(\textrm{mod}\:115).$ To find the inverse of $37\,(\textrm{mod}\:115),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 115 & = & 37\cdot 3 & + & 4 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 4 &=& 115 - 37\cdot 3\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 37 & = & 4\cdot 9 & + & 1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 37 - 4\cdot 9\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 4 & = & 4\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 28\cdot 37 - 9\cdot 115 \]

We can write this result in modulo $115,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 28\cdot 37 - 9\cdot 115 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:115)\\[5pt] 28\cdot 37 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:115) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $37$ modulo $115$ is $28.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $28,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 37x &\equiv 7 && (\text{mod}\:115) \\[5pt] 28\cdot 37x &\equiv 28\cdot 7 && (\text{mod}\:115) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 196 && (\text{mod}\:115) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 115\cdot 1 + 81&& (\text{mod}\:115) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 81 && (\text{mod}\:115) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 81 \: (\text{mod}\:115).$

But our original congruence was modulo $575$ (not modulo $115$). To find all the solutions modulo $575,$ we repeatedly add $115$ to $81$ modulo $575$ until we reach the number $81$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 81 && (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 81+115 \equiv 196 && (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 196+115 \equiv 311&& (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 311+115 \equiv 426&& (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 426+115 \equiv 541&& (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] x_6 &\equiv 541+115 \equiv 656 \equiv 575 + 81 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:575) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3,4,5}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{81}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{196}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{311}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{426}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{541} \: (\text{mod}\:575). \]

question.text:
Find the solutions of $78x \equiv 4 \:(\text{mod}\:406).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $406,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(78,406) =2.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=78$ and $n=406$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(78,406)=2. \] Since $b=4$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 78x &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:406) \\[5pt] 2\cdot 39x &\equiv 2\cdot 2 && (\text{mod}\:2\cdot 203) \\[5pt] \cancel 2\cdot 39x &\equiv \cancel 2\cdot 2 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 2\cdot 203) \\[5pt] 39x &\equiv 2 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=39$ and $n_1=203$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(39,203)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $203.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $39\,(\textrm{mod}\:203).$ To find the inverse of $39\,(\textrm{mod}\:203),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 203 & = & 39 \cdot 5 & + & 8 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 8 &=& 203 - 39\cdot 5\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 39 & = & 8\cdot 4 & + &7 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 7 &=& 39 - 8\cdot 4\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 8 & = & 7\cdot 1 & + &1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 8 - 7\cdot 1\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 7 & = & 7\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 5\cdot 203 -26\cdot 39 \]

We can write this result in modulo $203,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 5\cdot 203 -26\cdot 39 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:203)\\[5pt] -26\cdot 39 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] (203-26)\cdot 39 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] 177\cdot 39 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:203) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $39$ modulo $203$ is $177.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $177,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 39x &\equiv 2 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] 177\cdot 39x &\equiv 177\cdot 2 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 354 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] x &\equiv203 + 151 && (\text{mod}\:203) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 151 && (\text{mod}\:203) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 151 \: (\text{mod}\:203).$

But our original congruence was modulo $406$ (not modulo $203$). To find all the solutions modulo $406,$ we repeatedly add $203$ to $151$ modulo $406$ until we reach the number $151$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 151 && (\text{mod}\:406) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 151+203 \equiv 354 && (\text{mod}\:406) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 354+203 \equiv 557 \equiv 406 + 151 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:406) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{151}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{354}, \: (\text{mod}\:406). \]

example.title: Using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm

question.text:
Find the solutions of $95x \equiv 50 \:(\text{mod}\:235).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $235,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(95,235) =5.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=95$ and $n=235$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(95,235)=5. \] Since $b=50$ is divisible by $5,$ our congruence has $5$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 95x &\equiv 50 && (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] 5\cdot 19x &\equiv 5\cdot 10 && (\text{mod}\:5\cdot 47) \\[5pt] \cancel 5\cdot 19x &\equiv \cancel 5\cdot 10 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 5\cdot 47) \\[5pt] 19x &\equiv 10 && (\text{mod}\:47) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=19$ and $n_1=47$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(19,47)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $47.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $19\,(\textrm{mod}\:47).$ To find the inverse of $19\,(\textrm{mod}\:47),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 47 & = & 19\cdot 2 & + & 9 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 9 &=& 47 - 19\cdot 2\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 19 & = & 9\cdot 2 & + & 1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 19 - 9\cdot 2\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 9 & = & 9\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 5\cdot 19 - 2\cdot 47 \]

We can write this result in modulo $47,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 5\cdot 19 - 2\cdot 47 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:47)\\[5pt] 5\cdot 19 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:47) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $19$ modulo $47$ is $5.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 19x &\equiv 10 && (\text{mod}\:47) \\[5pt] 5\cdot 19x &\equiv 5\cdot 10 && (\text{mod}\:47) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 50 && (\text{mod}\:47) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 47\cdot 1 + 3&& (\text{mod}\:47) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 3 && (\text{mod}\:47) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 3 \: (\text{mod}\:47).$

But our original congruence was modulo $235$ (not modulo $47$). To find all the solutions modulo $235,$ we repeatedly add $47$ to $3$ modulo $235$ until we reach the number $3$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 3 && (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 3+47 \equiv 50 && (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 50+47 \equiv 97&& (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 97+47 \equiv 144&& (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 144+47 \equiv 191&& (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] x_6 &\equiv 191+47 \equiv 238 \equiv 235 + 3 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:235) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3,4,5}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{3}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{50}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{97}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{144}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{191} \: (\text{mod}\:235). \]

question.text:
Find the solutions of $132x \equiv 12 \:(\text{mod}\:441).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $441,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(132,441) =3.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=132$ and $n=441$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(132,144)=3. \] Since $b=12$ is divisible by $3,$ our congruence has $3$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 132x &\equiv 12 && (\text{mod}\:441) \\[5pt] 3\cdot44x &\equiv 3\cdot4 && (\text{mod}\:3\cdot147) \\[5pt] \cancel 3\cdot44x &\equiv \cancel 3\cdot4 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 3\cdot147) \\[5pt] 44x &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=4$ and $n_1=147$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(4,147)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $147.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $44\,(\textrm{mod}\:147).$ To find the inverse of $44\,(\textrm{mod}\:147),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 147 & = & 3 \cdot 44 & + & 15 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 15 &=& 147 - 3\cdot 44\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 44 & = & 15\cdot 2 & + &14 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 14 &=& 44 - 15\cdot 2\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 15 & = & 14\cdot 1 & + &1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 15 - 14\cdot 1\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 14 & = & 14\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 3\cdot 147 -10\cdot 44 \]

We can write this result in modulo $147,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 3 \cdot 147 - 10 \cdot 44 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:147)\\[5pt] -10\cdot 44 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] (147-10)\cdot 44 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] 137\cdot 44 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:147) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $44$ modulo $147$ is $137.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $137,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 44x &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] 137\cdot 44x &\equiv 137\cdot 4 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 548 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 3\cdot 147 + 107 && (\text{mod}\:147) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 107 && (\text{mod}\:147) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 107 \: (\text{mod}\:147).$

But our original congruence was modulo $441$ (not modulo $147$). To find all the solutions modulo $441,$ we repeatedly add $147$ to $107$ modulo $441$ until we reach the number $107$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 107 && (\text{mod}\:441) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 107+147 \equiv 254 && (\text{mod}\:441) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 254+147 \equiv 401&& (\text{mod}\:441) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 401+147 \equiv 548 \equiv 441 + 107 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:441) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{107}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{254}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{401} \: (\text{mod}\:441). \]

question.text:
Find the solutions of $122x \equiv 20 \:(\text{mod}\:514).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $514,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(122,514) =2.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=122$ and $n=514$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(122,514)=2. \] Since $b=20$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 122x &\equiv 20 && (\text{mod}\:514) \\[5pt] 2\cdot 61x &\equiv 2\cdot 10 && (\text{mod}\:2\cdot 257) \\[5pt] \cancel 2\cdot 61x &\equiv \cancel 2\cdot 10 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 2\cdot 257) \\[5pt] 61x &\equiv 10 && (\text{mod}\:257) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=61$ and $n_1=257$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(61,257)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $257.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $61\,(\textrm{mod}\:257).$ To find the inverse of $61\,(\textrm{mod}\:257),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 257 & = & 61 \cdot 4 & + & 13 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 13 &=& 257 - 61\cdot 4\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 61 & = & 13\cdot 4 & + &9 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 9 &=& 61 - 13\cdot 4\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 13 & = & 9\cdot 1 & + &4 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 4 &=& 13 - 9\cdot 1\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 9 & = & 4\cdot 2 & + &1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 9 - 4\cdot 2\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 4 & = & 4\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 59\cdot 61 -257\cdot 14 \]

We can write this result in modulo $257,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 59\cdot 61 -257\cdot 14 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:257)\\[5pt] 59\cdot 61 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:257) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $61$ modulo $257$ is $59.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $59,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 61x &\equiv 10 && (\text{mod}\:257) \\[5pt] 59\cdot 61x &\equiv 59\cdot 10 && (\text{mod}\:257) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 590 && (\text{mod}\:257) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 257\cdot 2 + 76 && (\text{mod}\:257) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 76 && (\text{mod}\:257) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 76 \: (\text{mod}\:257).$

But our original congruence was modulo $514$ (not modulo $257$). To find all the solutions modulo $514,$ we repeatedly add $257$ to $76$ modulo $514$ until we reach the number $76$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 76 && (\text{mod}\:514) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 76+257 \equiv 333 && (\text{mod}\:514) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 333+257 \equiv 590 \equiv 514 + 76 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:514) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{76}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{333} \: (\text{mod}\:514). \]
